correctness.rationale: For every m>=3 and every q>0, list the radius-0, radius-1 and whole-star weighted ball averages. For a nonnegative input shift by its hub value to obtain x_i, global offset A=(sum x_i)/(m+q), and pair coefficient t=1/(1+q). When A>=0 all variation comes from (x_i-A)_+ and the bound B=1-1/(m+q) follows. When A<0, positive deviations contribute P and negative deviations contribute min(t v_i,(N-P)/(m+q)); if P=0 the bound is t, and if P>0 the number k of negative leaves lies between 1 and m-1, giving coefficients at most B. Leaf and hub indicators exactly attain B and t. The strictly increasing/decreasing branches intersect at the stated unique quadratic root. The independent exact-rational verifier passed 19568 graph-ball and optimization tests; this is not the proof.

originality.rationale: The 2014 paper works with counting-measure graph maximal norms, the 2015 work with lattice variation, and the two 2020 finite-star articles with counting measure. The exact 2020 1-variation constant m/(m+1) is the q=1 special case and is not claimed as new. The new sharp dependence on arbitrary hub-to-leaf mass q>0 for every m>=3 and its unique balance point cannot be inferred from those specializations. Accessible earlier three-vertex weighted calculations cover m=2 but no m>=3. An uncatalogued weighted-star formula remains a genuine priority risk; searches are evidence, not a proof of novelty.
residual_risks: Unindexed or unpublished analyses of maximal operators on vertex-weighted stars may imply the formula.
Full text of Liu–Xue 2021 was not inspected and therefore cannot be categorically assessed as NOT_COVERING; available abstract does not make the exact parameter comparison decisive.
The three-vertex arbitrary-mass result is a neighboring case, not the same degree range; formal originality beyond that case may be viewed as a natural generalization.

value.rationale: Nonuniform vertex masses alter centered local and global averages while the graph BV seminorm remains fixed. The complete sharp two-parameter degree and hub-mass law identifies a genuine phase switch between spatially opposite extremizers and solves a natural mass calibration problem with a unique solution for all m>=3. It is more than a single enumerated small-graph constant and exhibits a distinct nonuniform minimizer, sharpening the known q=1 benchmark.
